clinicalPearls: A congenital myopathy defined histologically by type 1 (slow) fibres being consistently smaller than type 2 fibres, without other structural lesions.
Genetically heterogeneous, with recognised causes in TPM3, ACTA1, SELENON (SEPN1), RYR1 and MYH7.
Presents with neonatal or infantile hypotonia and proximal weakness, often with facial weakness, an elongated myopathic face and a high-arched palate.
Contractures, spinal rigidity and scoliosis may develop; associated external ophthalmoplegia points to particular genotypes.
Respiratory muscle weakness can be disproportionate to limb weakness, particularly with SELENON-related disease.
Diagnosis relies on quantitative morphometry showing type 1 fibres roughly 35 to 40 per cent smaller than type 2 fibres.
Type 1 fibre predominance commonly accompanies the disproportion.
The course is usually static or slowly progressive and strength may improve through childhood.
reference.pathophysiology: Congenital fibre type disproportion is a pathological pattern rather than a single disease, in which slow type 1 myofibres fail to reach normal size relative to fast type 2 fibres. The underlying mutations affect thin-filament and sarcomeric proteins such as tropomyosin, actin and slow myosin, the ryanodine receptor calcium-release channel, or selenoprotein N involved in redox regulation of calcium handling. These disturb fibre-type maturation and trophic regulation, impairing contractile function and producing the characteristic size discrepancy.
additionalDifferentials: Secondary type 1 fibre smallness (for example myotonic dystrophy)
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with fibre-type morphometry using ATPase or immunohistochemistry
Targeted or panel gene testing (TPM3, ACTA1, SELENON, RYR1, MYH7)
Pulmonary function testing and overnight respiratory monitoring
Spinal and skeletal imaging for scoliosis and contractures
redFlags: Respiratory decline out of proportion to limb weakness
reference.prognosis: Most cases are non-progressive or slowly progressive, with stable or slowly improving strength. Respiratory insufficiency is the principal determinant of morbidity and mortality, especially in SELENON-related disease.
pitfalls: Diagnosing the disorder without excluding secondary causes of type 1 fibre smallness.
Underestimating respiratory involvement because limb strength appears preserved.
Not pursuing a genetic diagnosis despite its prognostic and cardiac implications with MYH7.
Missing malignant hyperthermia susceptibility when RYR1 is involved.
references: Dubowitz V, Sewry CA, Oldfors A. Muscle Biopsy: A Practical Approach
International consensus guidance on the congenital myopathies
management: No specific drug therapy is available; care is supportive, with physiotherapy and occupational therapy to maintain strength, joint range and function

Prioritise respiratory monitoring with pulmonary function testing and overnight oximetry, and provide non-invasive ventilation for hypoventilation, which may be disproportionate to limb weakness in SELENON-related disease
Manage spinal rigidity, scoliosis and contractures with orthoses, stretching and orthopaedic or spinal surgery when indicated
Undertake anaesthetic risk assessment and avoid triggering agents where RYR1 malignant-hyperthermia susceptibility is possible
Arrange cardiac surveillance with echocardiography where MYH7 is implicated
Support nutrition and swallowing and assess for ophthalmoplegia in relevant genotypes
Offer genetic counselling for the mixed dominant and recessive inheritance and coordinate multidisciplinary neuromuscular follow-up
